editorial:
Imagine stepping back into the late eighties and diving into a world of grainy film and moody sounds. You get to experience a unique collection of music videos that feel more like short art films than typical pop clips. Everything is shot on Super-8 film, which gives it a raw, gritty look that fits the band's dark electronic style perfectly. Most of the footage is in black and white, but you will spot a few bright red megaphones that really pop against the grey backgrounds. It feels like a dream or a memory from a different era, making the whole experience feel very intimate and stylized.

What really works here is the vision of Anton Corbijn. He captures the band in a way that feels lonely yet powerful. The pacing is slow and steady, letting you soak in the images while the music does the heavy lifting. One of the biggest draws is the video for Pimpf, which you cannot find anywhere else. If you love synth-pop or old-school art, you need to see this. Since it is a vintage collection, try to find a high-quality digital remaster to stream or add the Blu-ray to your physical collection for the best detail.
endingExplained: The collection wraps up with the instrumental track Pimpf. Instead of a big plot twist, the ending serves as a visual mood piece. You see final, lingering shots that tie together the themes of isolation and industrial landscapes seen throughout the other videos. It doesn't have a traditional story ending, but it leaves you feeling a sense of closure by fading out into a quiet, empty space, mirroring the end of the album.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves 80s music and experimental art films.
